note: The measurements ByteMe offers. One shared list: the website (app.js) and the Python scripts (build_world.py, tests) both read it. 'code' is the NASA POWER parameter name. 'scale' multiplies the raw value (soil wetness 0-1 becomes percent). 'percent' says whether a percent change makes sense (zero means 'none of it'). Search: 'phrases' (several words, strong match) and 'keywords' (single words) link a question to a measurement. Avoid very general words such as water, air or ground: they appear in questions about many measurements. 'not_available' lists things people ask for that this data set does not have, with what to say and the closest measurement we do have. Measurements with "dataset": "nasa" come from data/nasa/ (built by build_nasa_grids.py); 'pair' names the NASA POWER measurement they double-check. 'related' lists measurements worth checking next (shown under an answer; never a claim about causes). 'drivers' lists possible drivers worth testing in Investigate (the Trend Decomposer), each with a one-line mechanism. They are suggestions to test, never claims about causes.

drivers.how: Sulfate from coal and oil burning is a large part of PM2.5.
Smoke from fires, stoves and traffic adds organic particles.
Dust blows in from dry land and deserts.
Calm air lets pollution build up; wind blows it away.
Rain washes particles out of the air.

guideline.text: the World Health Organization's guideline for the yearly average (5 µg/m³)

variables.name: Soot (black carbon) at ground level
variables.definition: How much soot (black carbon from diesel engines, coal and wood stoves, and fires) is in the air at ground level. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
variables.phrases: black carbon, soot particles, diesel exhaust, diesel fumes, chimney smoke, stove smoke, soot at ground level, black carbon at ground level
variables.examples: black soot from diesel engines and chimneys, dark smoke particles in city air

drivers.how: Traffic and burning give off soot and NO₂ together.
Fires add soot.

variables.name: Organic smoke particles at ground level
variables.definition: How much organic particle matter (from wildfires, burning crops and wood, traffic, and gases given off by plants) is in the air at ground level. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
variables.phrases: organic carbon, organic particles, organic aerosol, smoke particles, wood smoke, burning crops, crop burning, stubble burning, smoke particles at ground level, organic particles at ground level
variables.examples: smoke particles from burning fields and wood stoves, haze from forest fires at ground level

drivers.how: Fires give off most of the organic particles in many places.
Hot dry spells dry out plants, which then burn more easily.

variables.name: Sulfate particles at ground level
variables.definition: How much sulfate (particles formed from the sulfur dioxide of coal and oil burning, ships and volcanoes) is in the air at ground level, counted with the ammonium that usually comes with it. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
variables.phrases: sulfate particles, sulphate particles, sulfate at ground, coal particles, sulfate particles at ground level, sulphate particles at ground level, sulfate at ground level
variables.examples: particles from coal power plants in the air we breathe, sulfur pollution at street level

drivers.how: Sulfate forms in the air from sulfur dioxide.
Rain washes sulfate out of the air.

variables.name: Fine dust at ground level
variables.definition: How much fine mineral dust (the PM2.5 part of desert and soil dust) is in the air at ground level. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
variables.phrases: fine dust, dust we breathe, dusty air, dust particles, dust at ground level
variables.examples: fine desert dust in the air people breathe, dusty air in dry cities

drivers.how: Stronger wind lifts more dust.
Wet topsoil holds its dust.
Rain washes dust out of the air.

variables.name: Sulfur dioxide at ground level (MERRA-2)
variables.definition: How much sulfur dioxide gas (SO₂, mostly from burning coal and oil, metal smelters, ships and volcanoes) is in the air at ground level. The model calculates it from emission inventories (lists of known sources), not from measurements of SO₂ itself, so it shows how known emissions changed. Shown from 2003, when two MODIS satellite instruments began to guide the model.
variables.phrases: sulfur dioxide at ground, sulphur dioxide at ground, so2 at ground, so2 near the ground, sulfur in the air we breathe, sulfur dioxide at ground level, sulphur dioxide at ground level
variables.examples: sulfur dioxide gas near the ground from power plants and smelters

drivers.how: Sulfur dioxide turns into sulfate particles.

variables.name: Carbon monoxide at ground level (MERRA-2)
variables.definition: How much carbon monoxide (CO, a poisonous gas from engines, stoves, industry and fires) is in the air at ground level, in parts per billion. The model calculates it from emission inventories (lists of known sources), not from measurements of CO itself.
variables.phrases: carbon monoxide at ground, co at ground level, carbon monoxide near the ground, exhaust gas, car fumes, carbon monoxide at ground level
variables.examples: carbon monoxide from car exhausts and stoves in the air at street level

drivers.how: Fires give off carbon monoxide.

variables.name: Sulfur dioxide (OMI satellite)
variables.definition: How much sulfur dioxide (SO₂, from coal power plants, metal smelters, oil fields and volcanoes) is in the lowest part of the air, measured from space by OMI, in Dobson units. Daily maps are averaged by month.
variables.phrases: sulfur dioxide, sulphur dioxide, sulfur pollution, sulphur pollution, volcanic gas, volcano gas, volcanic gases, volcano gases
variables.examples: sulfur dioxide gas from coal plants and volcanoes seen from space
variables.low_note: Here there is very little SO₂ (on average below 0.15 Dobson units), within the noise of OMI's measurement. Trends at such low levels can come from the instrument rather than the air, so this result is not reliable. SO₂ trends are most meaningful near power plants, smelters and volcanoes.

variables.name: Formaldehyde (OMI satellite)
variables.definition: How much formaldehyde (HCHO) is in the air column, measured from space by OMI. It forms from gases given off by forests, fires, traffic and industry, so it shows where those gases (volatile organic compounds) are. Daily maps are averaged by month.
variables.phrases: volatile organic, organic gases, organic compounds
variables.examples: formaldehyde gas from forests, fires and factories seen from space
variables.product: OMHCHOd v003 (daily, every 5th 0.1° pixel, averaged by month)
variables.low_note: Here formaldehyde is low (on average below 2 × 10¹⁵ molecules/cm²), close to the noise of OMI's measurement, so small trends are not reliable. Formaldehyde trends are most meaningful over forests, fire regions and big cities.

drivers.how: Plants give off more of the gases that make formaldehyde when it is hot.
Fires give off formaldehyde.

variables.name: Smoke and dust index (OMI satellite)
variables.definition: OMI's ultraviolet aerosol index: how much smoke and dust that absorbs sunlight is in the air, seen from space. Values above about 1 mean a lot of smoke or dust; values near 0 or below mean clean air or only bright particles. Daily maps are averaged by month.
variables.phrases: aerosol index, uv aerosol index, smoke and dust, smoke or dust, absorbing aerosol, smoky air
variables.examples: smoke and dust clouds seen from space, plumes from fires and dust storms
variables.product: OMAERUVd v003 (UVAerosolIndex, daily, averaged by month)

drivers.how: Desert dust absorbs ultraviolet light.
Smoke absorbs ultraviolet light.

River flow and floods aren't in our data set; 'Runoff (GLDAS)' shows the water draining off the land.
